rv.q: The new production of 'Anything Goes' is a sublime spectacle that captures the effervescent spirit of Cole Porter's maritime musical with style and panache.
The girl's definitely got it and this gorgeously sung, buoyantly staged show is bliss.
This new “Anything Goes” is a daffy, shipshape romp.
The new Broadway revival of 'Anything Goes' is a hugely entertaining show that gets just about everything right.
When she leads the show-stopping “Blow, Gabriel, Blow,” you figure that if no horn-tooting archangel appears, it’s only because he’s afraid of the competition.
Massive tri-level tap formations, old fashioned vaudeville bawdry, and daffy costume-switches still do the trick
This splendid revival of Cole Porter's 1934 musical comedy is a joyous celebration of the kind of theatrical craftsmanship that made Broadway synonymous with quality entertainment.
And this production, the first on Broadway since Patti LuPone headlined a revival in 1987, has all that — plus an excellent cast led by the indefatigable Sutton Foster.

Though nearly a quarter century may be an eternity for people who love this Depression-genre nonsense, even they might wish the revival were blazing with justification for another run through the glittery Porter songbook.
With her fizzy enthusiasm and Girl Scout pluck, Foster doesn't feel quite right for Reno, a jawbreaker candy filled with 100-proof liquor.
This new production of Anything Goes is exactly what a Broadway revival should be: a glorious celebration of everything that made the original so special.
This gorgeously crafted revival is simultaneously sly and sweet: The show's jokes at the expense of a celebrity-mad culture ought to jump out at a contemporary, reality-TV-glutted audience.
In the end, Anything Goes offers what many theatergoers are looking for today: a lot of bang for the bloated Broadway buck and a chance to see a true star in action.

Kathleen Marshall's lavish production occasionally feels labored. But for the most part, to quote one of the musical's most famous lyrics, 'it's delightful, it's delicious, it's de-lovely.' Her choreography manages to turn almost every production number into a showstopper.
This production of Anything Goes is a buoyant, exuberant celebration that captures both the sophistication and silliness of Porter's era.
Director/choreographer Kathleen Marshall completes the picture with her knockout staging of the two biggest numbers.

It's just a glorified excuse for musicalizing and hijinks.
There is just not enough chemistry on this stage for anything dangerous (thrilling) to ignite.
With her eyes constantly darting around as if unsure of her place on the stage, Foster seems uncharacteristically out of sync both physically and vocally with her partners.
The revival of Cole Porter's Anything Goes is a joyous celebration of old-fashioned Broadway pizzazz.

Long after viewers forget the story, they’ll recall with pleasure the infernally catchy title number as choreographed by Marshall into an exuberantly tap-happy extravaganza that involves nearly the entire 28-member company led by Foster’s saucy Reno Sweeney.
Not everyone in the large supporting cast is up to her level.

cn.t: Critics hail this buoyant revival as old-fashioned musical comedy done right, with Sutton Foster's powerhouse performance and Kathleen Marshall's vibrant choreography delivering Cole Porter's classic with style, energy, and infectious joy.

sg.ra: SeatPlan and Headout consistently name Center Orchestra rows C-G as the sweet spot at this 2009 new-build Roundabout house, which was excavated up to 70 feet below street level to fit two-thirds of its seating on the orchestra level; the compressed footprint keeps C-G closer to the stage than most Broadway orchestras of equivalent row letter.

SeatPlan explicitly calls rows H-L the Orchestra's value zone, and Headout prices them around $115-120. A Sondheim-specific perk: row E was removed from the Left and Right Orchestra blocks, so SeatPlan notes row F (and by extension the H-L rows behind it) benefits from extra aisle-row stretch space. The mezz overhang does not start until around row K/L per BWW Forum and SeatPlan, so most of this band is still un-overhung.

A BWW Forum thread flags Left Orchestra row C as 'really really to the side - in an obstructed view sort of way,' and a TripAdvisor reviewer in Left Side Orchestra Row A during Beautiful reported the onstage piano blocked the right side of the stage while side-actor action on the left was cut off. Because the Sondheim auditorium was rebuilt underground in 2009 around the preserved 1918 facade, the side blocks wrap tight to the proscenium and are more angled than typical Shubert-era houses.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine AA-BB 'highly prized for their unbeatable overhead views of the stage, perfect for watching a musical,' and Headout echoes that front-mezz rows are preferred over orchestra front rows by some patrons thanks to the elevation. The mezz is unusually compact here (around 328-357 seats) because the entire auditorium is an underground 2009 LEED rebuild designed by Fisher Dachs / COOKFOX with a steep modern rake, so even AA-BB feel close despite being upstairs.

SeatPlan credits the mezz's 'good rake' for letting patrons at the back still 'get a clean view down to the stage,' and Headout names rows CC and FF as value picks. Because the Sondheim was rebuilt to modern sightline specs in 2009 (Fisher Dachs, LEED-certified), there are no legacy pillars like older Shubert-era houses — obstructions here are angular (side mezz) rather than structural.
